usage: The single most common collocation; Koreans 가격 비교 ('price comparison') before any purchase.
The second item takes 와/과 (or casual 하고/랑): 이걸 저거와 비교해요.
서로 ('mutually') is the natural adverb when two sides are weighed against each other.
Adding 보다 ('try and see') softens it to 'have a look and compare', e.g. 한번 비교해 보세요.
examples: 저는 가격을 비교해요
I compare prices
The plainest frame: object + 을/를 + 비교해요, an everyday shopping habit.
사기 전에 두 제품을 비교해 봤어요
Before buying, I compared the two products
사기 전에 ('before buying') + 비교해 봤어요 ('tried comparing') is exactly how a shopper talks.
남의 아이와 비교하지 마세요
Please don't compare (your child) with others' children
남(의) ('other people's') + 와 + 비교하지 마세요 — a heartfelt request, the social side of this verb.
nuance: 비교하다 is the Sino-Korean verb 比較(비교, 'compare-contrast') + 하다, meaning to set two or more things side by side to weigh their differences. The thing(s) compared take 을/를, and the second item of a pair takes 와/과 (formal) or 하고/랑 (casual): A를 B와 비교하다. Being a 하다 verb it conjugates to 해요 (never 하요) and 했어요. Distinguish it from 대조하다 (對照, 'contrast'), which highlights opposites for academic effect, while 비교하다 is the neutral everyday word ('compare prices, compare two phones'). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners copy English 'compare A to B' and say 가격에 비교해요, but the object marker must be 을/를 — 가격을 비교해요. Note too the social weight of 비교당하다 ('to be compared', passive): Koreans dislike being measured against others, so 비교하지 마 ('stop comparing me') is emotionally loaded.

mistakes: Saying 가격에 비교해요 with 에, copied from English 'compare to'. The thing compared is a direct object, so it must take 을/를: 가격을 비교해요.
Writing the present tense as 비교하요. Every 하다 verb contracts 하 + 여 to 해, so the form is 비교해요 / 비교했어요, never 비교하요.
Marking the second item of a pair with 을/를 too (이것을 저것을 비교해요). The compared-against partner takes 와/과: 이것을 저것과 비교해요.

usage: Object + 을/를 + 선택하다; 하나만 선택하세요 ('pick only one') is standard quiz/form wording.
Ubiquitous on screens and kiosks; 옵션을 선택하다 works the same way.
신중하게 ('prudently') is the adverb for weighty decisions; 마음대로 선택하다 = choose freely.
중에(서) ('among') marks the pool you pick from: 이 중에서 선택해요.
examples: 저는 파란색을 선택했어요
I chose the blue one
Plain object frame: color + 을/를 + 선택했어요, e.g. picking a phone case.
키오스크에서 메뉴를 선택해 주세요
Please select your menu on the kiosk
에서 ('at/on') the kiosk + 선택해 주세요 — exactly what a café screen tells you.
둘 다 좋아서 하나를 선택하기 어려워요
Both are good, so it's hard to pick one
선택하기 어렵다 ('hard to choose') turns the verb into a noun with -기.
nuance: 선택하다 is 選擇(선택, 'select-pick') + 하다 and means to pick a defined option from a presented set — menus, app settings, multiple-choice answers, life paths. It is the bookish, neutral register; in spoken everyday Korean the native verb 고르다 ('pick out') is warmer and more common ('과일을 골랐어요'). Crucially, contrast it with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide'): 선택하다 is choosing one option among several that already exist, while 결정하다 is settling a matter or reaching a conclusion ('유학을 결정했어요' = decided to study abroad). As a 하다 verb it gives 선택해요 / 선택했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the 고르다 split: say 메뉴를 선택해요 with 을/를 (not 메뉴에), and don't force 선택하다 into casual chat where a native would simply say 골라요. Also, 'choose to do X' is not 선택하다 alone — Korean prefers ~기로 하다/결심하다.

mistakes: Using 선택하다 to translate every English 'choose', including 'I chose to stay'. For 'choose to do', Korean uses ~기로 하다: 남기로 했어요, not 남는 것을 선택했어요.
Marking the option with 에 (메뉴에 선택해요) under the influence of English. The chosen thing is a direct object: 메뉴를 선택해요.
Treating 선택하다 and 결정하다 as interchangeable. 선택하다 = pick an existing option; 결정하다 = decide/settle a matter. 'I decided' is 결정했어요.

usage: The core grammar: 끊기로 결심했어요 ('resolved to quit'). The -기로 is almost obligatory.
굳게 ('firmly') and 단단히 are the signature adverbs of determination.
Idiomatic intransitive partner: 결심이 섰어요 ('my mind is made up').
굳히다 ('harden') collocates with the noun 결심 to mean cementing a decision.
examples: 저는 한국어를 배우기로 결심했어요
I resolved to learn Korean
Textbook frame: V-기로 결심했어요, a goal you set for yourself.
새해부터 운동하기로 굳게 결심했어요
I firmly resolved to exercise from the new year
새해부터 ('from the new year') + 굳게 — a classic resolution sentence.
여러 번 망설이다가 결국 결심했어요
After hesitating several times, I finally made up my mind
망설이다가 ('hesitating and then') + 결국 ('in the end') shows the inner struggle this verb implies.
nuance: 결심하다 is 決心(결심, 'decide-heart', literally 'fix the heart') + 하다, so it is not a neutral 'decide' but a determined, willpower-charged resolve — the New-Year-resolution verb. The indispensable pattern is V-기로 결심하다 ('make up one's mind to do V'): 담배를 끊기로 결심했어요. Contrast it sharply with 결정하다 (決定, 'decide-settle'): 결정하다 settles an external matter and can be about logistics or other people ('회의 날짜를 결정했어요' = decided the meeting date), whereas 결심하다 is always your own inner determination about your own action — you can't 결심하다 someone else's schedule. It is also stronger than casual 마음먹다, which feels homier. As a 하다 verb: 결심해요 / 결심했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping -기로 (saying 운동 결심했어요) and overusing 결심하다 for trivial choices; for 'I decided to have pasta tonight' Koreans just say 파스타 먹기로 했어요, reserving 결심하다 for serious resolve.

mistakes: Dropping the -기로 connector: 운동하기 결심했어요 or 운동 결심했어요. The verb you resolve to do must end in -기로: 운동하기로 결심했어요.
Using 결심하다 for routine decisions like picking a restaurant. It signals strong willpower; for light choices use ~기로 하다 (점심 먹기로 했어요).
Swapping it with 결정하다 when settling an external matter. 'We decided the date' is 날짜를 결정했어요, not 결심했어요 — 결심 is personal inner resolve only.

usage: to look forward to a trip
Object + 을/를 + 기대하다 for the happy-anticipation sense.
to expect a lot / look forward eagerly
많이 and 잔뜩 ('loads') intensify; 너무 기대하지 마 = don't get your hopes too high.
to be looked forward to / be exciting
The intransitive partner: 내일이 기대가 돼요 ('I'm excited for tomorrow').
Set phrase with the noun 기대 + 에 부응하다, common in formal/work speech.
examples: 저는 주말을 기대해요
I'm looking forward to the weekend
Plain frame; the hopeful, positive flavor of the verb.
이번 영화 정말 기대돼요
I'm really excited for this movie
기대돼요 (from 기대되다) describes the feeling rising in you, no object needed.
너무 기대하면 실망할 수도 있어요
If you expect too much, you might be disappointed
기대하면 ('if you expect') + 실망하다 pairs hope with its risk.
nuance: 기대하다 is 期待(기대, 'period-await', i.e. 'await a hoped-for time') + 하다, and unlike English 'expect' it leans positive: it means to anticipate something good and look forward to it. The thing awaited takes 을/를 (여행을 기대해요). Its hugely common intransitive twin 기대되다/기대가 되다 ('to be exciting, to be looked forward to') describes the feeling welling up in you — 내일이 기대돼요 — and beginners must keep the two apart: you 기대하다 a thing, but a thing/situation 기대된다 to you. Contrast with 기다리다 ('wait'), which is just neutral temporal waiting with no hope ('버스를 기다려요'); and with 바라다 ('wish/hope') which is a desire without the sense of confident anticipation. As a 하다 verb: 기대해요 / 기대했어요. The pitfall: English speakers map 'expect' onto neutral or negative situations ('I expect rain', 'I expect you to be late') — Korean 기대하다 cannot carry that. For neutral prediction use 예상하다 (豫想); 기대하다 is only for things you hope will be good.

Treating it as 기다리다. 'I'm waiting for the bus' is 버스를 기다려요 (neutral waiting), whereas 기대하다 adds hopeful excitement and can't replace it.

usage: Object + 을/를 + 상상하다; the object is a scene/picture in the mind.
상상해 보세요 ('just imagine') is the friendly, invitational default.
Emphatic idiom with 도 ('even'): 상상도 못 했어요 = it was unthinkable.
자유롭게 ('freely') fits creative contexts; 마음껏 상상하다 = imagine to your heart's content.
examples: 저는 가끔 여행을 상상해요
I sometimes imagine traveling
가끔 ('sometimes') + object frame — a pleasant daydream.
10년 후의 모습을 상상해 보세요
Try imagining how you'll be in 10 years
후의 모습 ('appearance after') + 상상해 보세요, a coaching-style prompt.
그런 일이 생길 줄은 상상도 못 했어요
I couldn't even imagine that would happen
상상도 못 하다 ('couldn't even imagine') is the natural way to express shock.
nuance: 상상하다 is 想像(상상, 'think-image', i.e. 'form a mental image') + 하다 — to picture in your mind something not present, from a fantasy to a hypothetical future. The thing imagined takes 을/를, and the gentle pattern 상상해 보세요 ('try to imagine') is far more natural than a bare command. Contrast it carefully with 생각하다 ('think'), which is broad reasoning, deliberation, or opinion, whereas 상상하다 specifically conjures a vivid image or scenario; '생각해 보세요' = think it over, but '상상해 보세요' = picture it. Also distinguish 공상하다 (空想, 'empty-imagine', daydreaming with a tinge of unreality) and 상상하다 (neutral, can be realistic planning). As a 하다 verb: 상상해요 / 상상했어요. The English-speaker pitfall: 'imagine that...' as a clause is handled with ~다고/는다고 상상하다 or just ~ㄴ/는 모습을 상상하다 (picture the scene), not a borrowed 'that' structure; and the very common 'I can't imagine' is idiomatically 상상도 못 하다 or 상상이 안 가다, not a literal 상상할 수 없다 in casual speech.

Saying 상상할 수 없어요 for everyday 'I can't imagine / unbelievable'. Natives prefer the idioms 상상도 못 했어요 or 상상이 안 가요.
Dropping the object particle (그 장면 상상해요). The pictured thing needs 을/를: 그 장면을 상상해요.

usage: Object of focus takes 에, not 을/를: 일에 집중하다, 수업에 집중하다.
to be able to focus well
Intransitive partner: 오늘은 집중이 안 돼요 ('I can't focus today').
정신(을) ('spirit/mind') is the thing you gather; here 을/를 marks 정신, while the target still takes 에.
Noun 집중력 ('focus power') + 높이다, common in study-tip talk.
examples: 저는 수업에 집중해요
I concentrate in class
수업에 ('on the class') — note 에, the signature particle of this verb.
시끄러워서 일에 집중할 수 없어요
It's noisy, so I can't concentrate on work
시끄러워서 ('because it's noisy') + 일에 집중하다 in a real distraction scene.
딱 30분만 집중해 봐요
Let's focus for just 30 minutes
딱 ... 만 ('exactly ... only') + 집중해 봐요, an encouraging study nudge.
nuance: 집중하다 is 集中(집중, 'gather-center', i.e. 'draw to a central point') + 하다 — to gather your attention onto one thing. Its defining grammar trait is the particle: the focus target takes 에 (공부에 집중하다, 일에 집중하다), NOT 을/를, because you are 'centering toward' a point. The intransitive 집중이 되다/안 되다 ('focus comes / won't come') is essential for everyday complaints: 집중이 안 돼요. Contrast it with 몰두하다 (沒頭, 'sink the head in'), which is deeper, more absorbed immersion ('연구에 몰두하다'), and with 신경 쓰다, which is worried attention rather than productive focus. As a 하다 verb: 집중해요 / 집중했어요. The big English-speaker pitfall is exactly the particle — learners say 공부를 집중해요 by analogy with a direct object, but it must be 공부에 집중해요. Also, English 'focus on doing X' becomes ~하는 데(에) 집중하다 (외우는 데 집중해요), not a borrowed gerund; and to tell someone to pay attention right now, the natural phrase is 집중하세요 or 집중 좀 해 ('focus, please').

Dropping the particle entirely (공부 집중해요). In careful speech the 에 should be there: 공부에 집중하다.
Using 집중하다 for worried/caring attention. 'I care about what others think' is 신경 써요, not 집중해요 — 집중하다 is productive mental focus, not worry.

usage: Object + 을/를 + 인정하다; 실수를 인정하다 ('admit a mistake') is the apology staple.
사실(을) ('the fact') + 인정하다 for accepting something as true.
Passive 인정받다 ('be acknowledged') is hugely common for earning respect.
순순히 ('compliantly') captures admitting without making excuses.
examples: 제 잘못을 인정해요
I admit my fault
Plain apology frame: 잘못을 인정하다, owning your error.
그 사람 실력은 인정할 수밖에 없어요
I have no choice but to acknowledge that person's skill
~ㄹ 수밖에 없다 ('can only') + 인정하다 = grudging recognition.
솔직히 인정할게요, 제가 틀렸어요
Honestly, I'll admit it — I was wrong
솔직히 ('frankly') + 인정할게요 ('I'll admit') in a candid confession.
nuance: 인정하다 is 認定(인정, 'recognize-fix', i.e. 'recognize as established') + 하다, covering two linked senses: to admit/own up to something (잘못을 인정하다 = admit a fault) and to acknowledge/recognize something or someone as valid (실력을 인정하다 = recognize ability). The object takes 을/를. Its passive 인정받다 ('to be recognized') is a high-value word — earning 인정 from others is a big social currency in Korea. In texting slang, 인정 (or ㅇㅈ) alone means 'true / agreed / fair point'. Contrast with 동의하다 ('agree'), which is sharing an opinion or consenting, whereas 인정하다 is conceding a truth even one you dislike — you can 인정하다 a rival's talent without 동의하다 their views; and with 자백하다 (自白, confess a crime), which is far heavier and legal. As a 하다 verb: 인정해요 / 인정했어요. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 에 (잘못에 인정해요) — it's 을/를; and note that 'admit defeat' is the set phrase 패배를 인정하다, while a flat 인정할 수 없어요 means 'I refuse to accept that', a firm rejection, not mere doubt.

structuredNuance.t: Covers two linked senses: to admit/own up to something (잘못을 인정하다 = admit a fault) and to acknowledge/recognize something or someone as valid (실력을 인정하다 = recognize ability). usage: What you agree with takes 에: 그 말에 동의해요, 생각에 동의해요.
The fixed phrase on every signup screen: 약관에 동의합니다.
전적으로 ('wholly') is the strong-agreement adverb; 부분적으로 동의하다 = partly agree.
Noun 동의 ('consent') + 구하다 ('seek'), common in formal/medical contexts.
examples: 저도 그 말에 동의해요
I agree with that too
도 ('also') + 말에 동의하다 — backing someone up in conversation.
서비스 이용약관에 동의하시겠습니까?
Do you agree to the terms of service?
약관에 동의하다 in its native habitat, the consent checkbox.
그 점에는 동의하지만 방법은 반대예요
I agree on that point, but I'm against the method
동의하지만 ('agree but') sets up a polite disagreement on the how.
nuance: 동의하다 is 同意(동의, 'same-meaning/intent') + 하다 — literally to be of the same mind, i.e. to agree with an opinion or consent to terms. Also contrast 인정하다 (concede a truth) — agreeing is positive alignment, acknowledging is conceding. As a 하다 verb: 동의해요 / 동의했어요. usage: Object + 을/를 + 받아들이다; 결과를 받아들이다 ('accept the outcome') is just as common.
제안(을) ('proposal') + 받아들이다 for saying yes to an offer.
있는 그대로 ('just as it is') is the set adverbial for accepting without changing.
겸허히 ('humbly') often pairs with accepting criticism: 비판을 겸허히 받아들이다.
examples: 저는 그 사실을 받아들여요
I accept that fact
Plain frame; note the contraction 이 + 어 → 여 in 받아들여요.
떨어졌지만 결과를 받아들이기로 했어요
I failed, but I decided to accept the result
받아들이기로 하다 ('decide to accept') shows coming to terms with it.
네 사과를 받아들일게요
I'll accept your apology
받아들일게요 ('I'll accept', speaker's intent) in a reconciliation.
nuance: 받아들이다 is a native compound, 받다 ('receive') + 들이다 ('let in / take inward'), so it literally means 'receive and let inside' — to take something in and come to terms with it: a fact, a result, an apology, criticism, a proposal. The object takes 을/를. Conjugation hinges on the stem ending in -이: 받아들이 + 어 contracts to 받아들여, giving 받아들여요 / 받아들였어요 (never the uncontracted 받아들이어요). Contrast it with 인정하다 (concede/recognize as true) — you can 인정하다 a harsh fact intellectually but still struggle to 받아들이다 it emotionally; and with plain 받다, which is the physical receiving of an object (선물을 받다 = receive a gift), whereas 받아들이다 is mental/emotional acceptance. Also note 수락하다 (受諾) as a formal synonym for accepting an offer. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use bare 받다 for 'accept an apology/criticism/situation' — that needs 받아들이다 (사과를 받아들이다); and remember the -여 contraction, since writing 받아들이어요 is a classic learner slip.

usage: to make up one's mind to do V
The core pattern: 끊기로 마음먹었어요 ('made up my mind to quit').
단단히 ('tightly') and 독하게 ('harshly') intensify the resolve.
마음먹으면 ('if/once you set your mind') heads a very common conditional about persistence.
Set saying: 모든 게 마음먹기에 달렸어요 ('it all comes down to your resolve').
examples: 저는 운동하기로 마음먹었어요
I made up my mind to exercise
V-기로 마음먹다 — the warm, everyday way to state a resolution.
한번 마음먹으면 끝까지 하는 성격이에요
Once I decide, I'm the type to see it through
마음먹으면 + 끝까지 ('to the end') describes a determined personality.
독하게 마음먹고 새벽 운동을 시작했어요
I steeled myself and started dawn workouts
독하게 마음먹다 ('resolve fiercely') conveys serious determination.
nuance: 마음먹다 is a vivid native idiom: 마음 ('heart/mind') + 먹다 ('eat'), literally 'to eat the mind' — to take a decision firmly inside you, i.e. make up your mind. The signature grammar is V-기로 마음먹다 (운동하기로 마음먹었어요). Although 먹다 here is figurative, it conjugates as the ordinary verb 먹다, giving 마음먹어요 / 마음먹었어요 / 마음먹으면. Compare it with 결심하다: both mean 'resolve', but 마음먹다 is homier, more conversational and gut-level, while Sino-Korean 결심하다 is a touch more formal and goal-oriented — a New Year's 결심 looks better on a list, but a friend would say 나 운동하기로 마음먹었어. Distinguish too from 작정하다 ('to be set/determined', often with a stubborn or even negative edge: 작정하고 덤비다 = come at it with full intent). The English-speaker pitfall: keep it as one word 마음먹다 in the 'resolve' sense — splitting it into 마음을 먹다 sounds odd; and don't drop -기로, since 운동 마음먹었어요 is ungrammatical. Note the proverb-like 마음먹기에 달렸다 ('it depends on your mindset'), great for encouragement.

usage: Object + 을/를 + 잊어버리다; 약속을 잊어버리다 ('forget an appointment') is a common slip.
to clean forget / slip one's mind
깜빡 ('in a flash') is the natural adverb for an absent-minded lapse.
다 ('all') + 잊어버리다 — often advice to let painful things go.
까맣게 (lit. 'blackly') is an idiom meaning forgotten without a trace.
examples: 저는 비밀번호를 잊어버렸어요
I forgot the password
Everyday frame; note the past 리 + 었 → 렸: 잊어버렸어요.
깜빡 잊어버리고 우산을 안 가져왔어요
It slipped my mind and I didn't bring an umbrella
깜빡 잊어버리고 ('forgetting in a flash, and...') chains to the consequence.
나쁜 기억은 다 잊어버리세요
Please forget all the bad memories
잊어버리세요 ('do forget') used kindly to help someone move on.
nuance: 잊어버리다 is the native compound 잊다 ('forget') + -어 버리다 (the auxiliary 버리다, 'throw away / do completely'), so it means to forget thoroughly, with the nuance that the memory is gone for good — often tinged with regret ('darn, it's gone'). Plain 잊다 states the bare fact of forgetting; 잊어버리다 adds finality and emotional color, which is why everyday speech overwhelmingly uses 잊어버리다. The object takes 을/를. Conjugation: the 리 stem contracts with 어 to 려, hence 잊어버려요 / 잊어버렸어요. The most dangerous English-speaker pitfall is the near-twin 잃어버리다 ('to lose a physical object'): 잊다 (forget, from the mind) vs 잃다 (lose, from your possession) differ by one jamo and one meaning — you 잊어버리다 a name but 잃어버리다 your wallet. Mixing them is the classic learner error. Also note: to tell someone 'don't forget', say 잊어버리지 마세요 or just 잊지 마세요; and writing the uncontracted 잊어버리었어요 is wrong — it must be 잊어버렸어요.

usage: The recalled thing takes 이/가, not 을/를: 단어가 생각나요.
갑자기 ('suddenly') fits the spontaneous, involuntary nature of the verb.
The base 생각이 나다 can split around adjectives: 좋은 생각이 났어요 ('a good idea came').
문득 ('all of a sudden, out of nowhere') is the literary-flavored partner adverb.
examples: 갑자기 고향이 생각나요
My hometown suddenly comes to mind
이/가 marks what surfaces in memory; the feeling arises on its own.
좋은 생각이 났어요!
I've got a good idea!
생각이 나다 split by 좋은 — the everyday 'I have an idea' exclamation.
아무리 해도 그 단어가 생각나지 않아요
No matter what, I just can't recall that word
아무리 해도 ('however much I try') + 생각나지 않다 = the tip-of-the-tongue feeling.
nuance: 생각나다 is 생각 ('thought') + 나다 ('arise / come out'), so it literally means 'a thought arises' — something comes to mind or you recall it spontaneously, without effort. This grammar is the heart of the word: because the memory surfaces by itself, the recalled thing is the SUBJECT and takes 이/가 (이름이 생각나요), not 을/를. Contrast it sharply with 생각하다 ('think'), which is volitional, active deliberation taking 을/를 (그 일을 생각해요 = I'm thinking about that): 생각하다 = you do the thinking; 생각나다 = a thought comes to you. Compare also 기억나다 ('a memory comes back', near-synonym, slightly more about stored memory) and 떠오르다 ('to float up', vivid for ideas/images suddenly emerging). 나다 is a regular verb: 생각나요 / 생각났어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the agency: learners translate 'I remember the name' as 이름을 생각나요 with an object, but Korean frames it as the name doing the surfacing — 이름이 생각나요. And 'I can't remember' is naturally the negative 생각이 안 나요 / 생각나지 않아요, not a 'can't' construction.

usage: What you mind about takes 에: 외모에 신경 쓰다, 디테일에 신경 쓰다.
The go-to reassurance phrase; casual 신경 쓰지 마 ('never mind it').
남의 시선('others' gaze') + 에 신경 쓰다 = caring what people think.
to take care (for someone), be thoughtful
써 주다 ('do the minding for') expresses gratitude: 신경 써 줘서 고마워요.
examples: 저는 옷차림에 신경 써요
I pay attention to how I dress
옷차림에 ('on one's outfit') + 신경 쓰다 — note the 에 particle.
그런 말은 신경 쓰지 마세요
Don't let that kind of comment bother you
신경 쓰지 마세요 used to comfort someone who's hurt.
다른 사람 눈치까지 신경 쓰느라 피곤해요
I'm tired from minding even other people's reactions
신경 쓰느라 ('busy minding, so...') links the caring to the exhaustion it causes.
nuance: 신경 쓰다 pairs the Sino-Korean noun 神經 (신경, 'nerve') with the verb 쓰다 ('use'), literally 'to use one's nerves' — to expend mental energy minding, caring about, or worrying over something. It spans neutral attention (디테일에 신경 쓰다 = pay attention to detail) and anxious preoccupation (남 눈치에 신경 쓰다 = fret over others' reactions). The object of concern takes 에 (or 에게/한테 for a person), not 을/를. Conjugation is a key trap: 쓰다 is a ㅡ-irregular, so the ㅡ drops before 어 — 쓰 + 어 → 써, giving 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요, never 신경 쓰어요. Contrast it with 걱정하다 ('worry'), which is pure anxiety about an outcome, whereas 신경 쓰다 is the act of devoting attention (which may or may not be worried); and with 관심 있다 ('be interested'), which is positive curiosity. The single most useful phrase is 신경 쓰지 마(세요) ('don't worry about it / never mind'), heard constantly. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 을/를 (그 일을 신경 써요) — say 그 일에 신경 써요; and don't reach for 돌보다 ('physically take care of, tend') when you mean mental attention — '나는 외모에 신경 써' is care/attention, not nursing.

Contrast it with 걱정하다 ('worry'), which is pure anxiety about an outcome, whereas 신경 쓰다 is the act of devoting attention (which may or may not be worried); and with 관심 있다 ('be interested'), which is positive curiosity.

쓰다 is a ㅡ-irregular, so the ㅡ drops before 어 — 쓰 + 어 → 써, giving 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요, never 신경 쓰어요.
Don't use 을/를 (그 일을 신경 써요) — say 그 일에 신경 써요; and don't reach for 돌보다 ('physically take care of, tend') when you mean mental attention — '나는 외모에 신경 써' is care/attention, not nursing.

mistakes: Marking the concern with 을/를 (그것을 신경 써요). 신경 쓰다 takes 에: 그것에 신경 써요 (people: 그 사람에게 신경 써요).
Ignoring the ㅡ-irregular and writing 신경 쓰어요 / 신경 쓰었어요. The ㅡ drops: 신경 써요 / 신경 썼어요.
Using 걱정하다 when you mean attentive minding. 신경 쓰다 = devote attention (possibly worried); 걱정하다 = be anxious about an outcome. 'I'm worried about the exam' is 시험이 걱정돼요.

usage: to pick up on the mood
Object + 을/를 + 알아채다; 변화를 알아채다 ('notice a change') is just as common.
금방 ('right away') and 바로 ('instantly') fit the sudden flash of realizing.
to take the hint / read the situation
Near-twin 눈치(를) 채다 ('catch the social cue') is the everyday cousin of this verb.
거짓말(을) ('a lie') + 알아채다 = detect that something is false.
examples: 저는 바로 알아챘어요
I noticed right away
Plain frame; note the past 채 + 었 → 챘: 알아챘어요.
아무도 제 실수를 못 알아챘어요
Nobody noticed my mistake
못 알아채다 ('fail to notice') — 못 negates ability, here a lucky escape.
표정만 보고 거짓말인 걸 알아챘어요
Just from your expression, I caught that it was a lie
~ㄴ 걸 알아채다 ('notice that it is...') takes a whole clause as the object.
nuance: 알아채다 is the native compound 알다 ('know') + 채다 ('snatch / catch quickly'), so it means to suddenly catch on to or become aware of something — often something subtle, hidden, or not openly stated (a lie, a mood shift, a hint). The object takes 을/를, and a whole situation can be its object via ~ㄴ/는 걸 알아채다 (거짓말인 걸 알아챘어요). Conjugation: the 채 stem contracts with past 었 to 챘, giving 알아챘어요 (not 알아채었어요). Contrast it with 눈치채다, an almost identical everyday synonym focused on reading social cues; the two are largely interchangeable, though 눈치채다 leans toward interpersonal/atmospheric cues. Distinguish it from 알아보다 (알다 + 보다, 'look into'), which means to recognize someone/something or to investigate ('얼굴을 알아보다' = recognize a face; '가격을 알아보다' = look into a price) — a different verb, not 'notice'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'notice that X' must be packaged as ~ㄴ/는 걸 알아채다 or ~다는 걸 알아채다, not a borrowed 'that'-clause; and don't confuse the lookalike 알아보다 — to notice/catch on is 알아채다, while to recognize or check into is 알아보다.

The native compound 알다 ('know') + 채다 ('snatch / catch quickly').
The 채 stem contracts with past 었 to 챘, giving 알아챘어요 (not 알아채었어요).

'notice that X' must be packaged as ~ㄴ/는 걸 알아채다 or ~다는 걸 알아채다, not a borrowed 'that'-clause; and don't confuse the lookalike 알아보다 — to notice/catch on is 알아채다, while to recognize or check into is 알아보다.

Writing the uncontracted past 알아채었어요. The 채 + 었 contracts to 챘: 알아챘어요.
Trying to attach an English 'that'-clause directly. 'I noticed that he lied' becomes 그가 거짓말한 걸 알아챘어요, using ~ㄴ 걸 to nominalize the clause.
